title: CDN, reverse proxy and load balancer
description: Learn how CDNs cache content close to users, how reverse proxies shield applications, and how load balancers distribute traffic across servers.

data.text: Modern web applications rarely serve users directly from a single origin server. Instead, traffic passes through **CDNs**, **reverse proxies**, and **load balancers** before reaching application code. Each layer solves a different problem: latency, protection, or capacity.
CDN: caching close to the user

A Content Delivery Network (CDN) stores copies of static assets at locations around the world. When a user requests a file, the CDN serves it from the nearest location instead of routing the request all the way to the origin server.

items: Reduces latency by serving from nearby data centers
Absorbs traffic spikes without hitting the origin
Often provides DDoS protection and WAF features
Common CDNs: Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, AWS CloudFront

data.title: Cache invalidation is hard
data.text: Changing a file on the origin does not automatically update the CDN copy. Use versioned filenames, short TTLs for dynamic content, or explicit purge APIs.
A reverse proxy sits between clients and your application server. It receives requests from the internet and forwards them to internal services. Clients usually do not know the proxy exists.

items: Hides internal server addresses and topology
Terminates TLS so application servers do not need certificates
Can compress responses, rewrite URLs, or block attacks
Common reverse proxies: Nginx, Apache, Caddy, Envoy

data.text: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers. It prevents any single server from becoming a bottleneck and improves availability by removing unhealthy servers from rotation.

items: Round-robin: distribute requests evenly
Least connections: send traffic to the least busy server
IP hash: route the same client to the same server
Health checks: stop sending traffic to failed servers

cards.title: Reverse proxy
cards.description: Routes requests to the correct backend service.
items: Hides backend servers
Handles TLS and caching
Often sits in front of multiple applications

cards.title: Load balancer
cards.description: Distributes requests across multiple instances of the same service.
items: Improves throughput and availability
Removes unhealthy instances
Can be hardware or software

data.title: They often overlap
data.text: In practice, reverse proxies and load balancers are frequently combined. Nginx, for example, can terminate TLS, cache content, and balance traffic across backends in a single layer.

data.title: Common traffic path
items: User requests `https://example.com`
DNS resolves to the CDN edge location
CDN serves static assets or forwards to the reverse proxy
Reverse proxy terminates TLS and forwards to the load balancer
Load balancer selects a healthy application server
Application server processes the request and returns data

data.caption: Typical layered architecture for a production web application
data.mermaid:
graph TD
    U[User] --> D[CDN]
    D -->|miss| P[Reverse Proxy]

data.title: Key takeaways
points: CDNs cache content near users to reduce latency and origin load.
Reverse proxies protect and simplify backend infrastructure.
Load balancers distribute traffic and remove failed servers.
These layers are often combined into unified infrastructure in production.
data.takeaway: Understanding CDNs, reverse proxies, and load balancers helps you design systems that scale, tolerate failures, and serve global audiences efficiently.

items.question: Do I need all three layers?
items.answer: Not always. A small site may use only a CDN. A mid-sized site may add a reverse proxy. Large systems typically combine all three for resilience and performance.

items.question: What is a WAF?
items.answer: A Web Application Firewall inspects HTTP traffic for attacks like SQL injection or cross-site scripting. Many CDNs and reverse proxies include WAF capabilities.

items.question: How does a load balancer know a server is healthy?
items.answer: It sends periodic health-check requests, often to a dedicated endpoint. If the endpoint returns an error or times out, the server is removed from the pool.

data.text: A layered edge architecture turns the internet itself into part of your application stack.
